opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think research acceleration evals are useful for a couple of reasons.

First, they measure something that actually matters. A lot of traditional benchmarks test narrow skills, like answering a multiple-choice question or solving a self-contained math problem. Those are informative, but they don't tell you directly whether a model can do the messy, open-ended work real researchers do. That means reading a codebase, forming a hypothesis, running experiments, debugging when things break, and deciding what to try next. Research acceleration evals try to capture that whole loop. So when a model improves on them, it's a much more meaningful signal about real-world usefulness.

Second, they matter a lot from a preparedness and safety perspective. One of the capabilities we care most about tracking is whether models can meaningfully speed up AI research itself. If models start substantially accelerating the work of building better models, the pace of progress could change in ways we want to see coming, not discover after the fact. Having concrete, grounded measurements of that, rather than vibes or anecdotes, helps us make better decisions about safeguards and deployment.

Third, they're hard to saturate. Real research tasks have a long tail of difficulty. There's always a harder experiment, a messier codebase, a more ambiguous goal. That gives the evals a longer shelf life than benchmarks that get maxed out within a few months of release.

And honestly, they're just exciting. When you see a model reproduce a result from a paper or find a bug a human missed, you get a real glimpse of how these systems could become genuine collaborators in science. Measuring that carefully is one of the best ways to understand where we are on that trajectory.

fable-5.1.text:
I think research acceleration evals are useful because they get at the thing we actually care about, which is not whether a model can answer a trivia question or pass some benchmark, but whether it can meaningfully speed up the people doing the hardest work. If you think about what it would mean for AI to really change the world, a lot of that runs through science and engineering. Can a model help a researcher go from an idea to a result faster? Can it help them find the right paper, write the experiment, debug the thing that's broken at two in the morning?

So when we build these evaluations, we try to mirror real research workflows. We take tasks that actual researchers have done, where we know what good looks like because someone has already produced the result, and we ask whether the model can do it, or how much of it, or how much it helps a human doing it. That gives you a signal that's grounded in reality rather than in a synthetic puzzle.

The other reason I like them is that they're honest about where models fall short. A lot of benchmarks saturate quickly and then stop telling you anything. Research tasks are long, messy, and require judgment across many steps, so there's a lot of headroom. When a model fails, you can usually see exactly where it fell apart, whether it was planning, or carrying context over a long horizon, or just making a subtle error that compounded. That's incredibly useful for understanding what to work on next.

And finally, from a safety and preparedness standpoint, this is one of the capabilities we most want to track carefully. If models start to substantially accelerate AI research itself, that changes the pace of everything, and we want to see that coming with as much warning as possible, measured rigorously rather than guessed at.

astra-6.text:
I find them useful because they get at a very concrete question: can an AI system help us make progress on research faster? That’s different from asking whether it can answer a question we already know the answer to. Research involves uncertainty—figuring out what to try, interpreting results, and deciding what to do next.

These evaluations can help us understand where a model actually contributes to that process. Does it save a researcher time? Does it suggest a useful experiment? Or does checking its work take more effort than it saves? That gives us a clearer picture of both what the model can do today and what needs to improve.

Research involves a lot of open-ended work—figuring out what question to ask, designing an experiment, interpreting a result—and a model can be strong at individual tasks without being useful across that whole process. These evaluations help us understand where it provides real assistance, where it still needs human guidance, and what’s preventing it from being more useful.
